title: Room Acoustical Parameters as Predictors of Acoustic Comfort in Outdoor Spaces of Housing Complexes
research_question: To what extent classic room acoustical parameters (STI, D50, C50, C80, EDT, LF80, EchoD) and A-weighted equivalent continuous sound level (LAeq) are able to predict perceived short-term acoustic comfort in outdoor spaces (i.e., courtyards) of virtual housing complexes, considering the effects of facade absorption, sound source, and observer position.

participants.description: Experiment 1: 27 subjects (7 females, 20 males, aged 19-57, median 38). Experiments 2 & 3: 42 subjects (13 females, 29 males, aged 18-64, median 41). All self-reported normal-hearing.
participants.recruitment: Most subjects worked for the authors' research institute.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Auralized stimuli from virtual inner yards (100x20x20m, unceiled, brick/concrete walls with glass windows) with varied facade absorption (reflecting, absorbing, exaggerated absorption, aw values 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.55, 0.95) and balcony ceiling absorption (aw values 0.05, 0.30, 0.95). Sound sources included bouncing basketball, doll's pram, German conversation, children playing, crying baby, Swiss German conversation. Stimuli were 8-10s long, normalized to LAeq of 50 dB(A) for ODEON input. Played back via 2D surround sound over 5 loudspeakers and 2 subwoofers.

findings.antecedent: Inner yard type (absorbing vs. reflecting facade setups)
findings.mechanism: Absorptive materials reduce sound pressure levels and reflections, leading to increased comfort.
findings.quote: Compared to the two reflecting inner yards, acoustic comfort was rated higher for the two absorbing inner yards, p < 0.001.

findings.antecedent: Sound source type (children sounds vs. other sources)
findings.mechanism: Relatively pleasant sounds (e.g., playing children) are associated with higher comfort.
findings.quote: Acoustic comfort was rated higher for the two children sounds than for the three other sound sources, all p < 0.001.

findings.antecedent: Observer position (20m in yard & second-floor balcony vs. 5m in yard)
findings.mechanism: Positions with lower sound pressure levels and/or weaker flutter echoes are more comfortable.
findings.quote: The observer positions at 20 m distance in the yard and at the second floor balcony were found to be "more" and "less" comfortable than the position at 5 m distance in the yard, respectively

findings.mechanism: Moderate absorption provides optimal acoustic conditions, while too little or too much absorption leads to lower comfort.
findings.quote: A parabolic relationship was found. That is, acoustic comfort was rated the highest for moderate (i.e., middle) aw values.
Balcony ceiling's aw was not found to affect acoustic comfort significantly, although such a non-significant tendency could be observed

findings.antecedent: Balcony ceiling's weighted absorption coefficient (aw) in absence of facade absorption
findings.mechanism: Absorbing materials on balcony ceilings can improve acoustic comfort as a simple solution.
findings.quote: Nevertheless, in the absence of any absorbers on the facade, absorbing balcony ceilings tended to improve acoustic comfort.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic comfort rating (very uncomfortable/comfortable vs. middle range)
findings.mechanism: Stronger affective responses (very uncomfortable or very comfortable) lead to faster, more automatic judgments.
findings.quote: That is, when subjects felt very uncomfortable or very comfortable, they gave their response faster than when they rated their comfort in response to the acoustic stimuli in the middle range of the scale.

findings.mechanism: Increased cumulative sound exposure level (LAE) with increasing playback sequence leads to lower acoustic comfort.
findings.quote: overall, acoustic comfort decreased slightly with increasing playback sequence.

findings.mechanism: Higher speech intelligibility contributes to perceived acoustic comfort.
Higher clarity of early sound energy contributes to perceived acoustic comfort.
Higher clarity of speech contributes to perceived acoustic comfort.
Higher clarity of music contributes to perceived acoustic comfort.
Longer early decay times (more reverberation) reduce perceived acoustic comfort.
Higher lateral energy fraction (more lateral reflections) reduces perceived acoustic comfort.
Inconsistent correlation across experiments, not a proper predictor.
findings.quote: Since the correlation between acoustic comfort and the EchoD is rather inconsistent... this criterion was considered not to be a proper predictor of acoustic comfort.

findings.mechanism: STI is a significant predictor of acoustic comfort in linear mixed-effect models.

C80 is a significant predictor of acoustic comfort in linear mixed-effect models.

findings.antecedent: A-weighted equivalent continuous sound level (LAeq) for unpleasant sound sources (Experiment 1)
findings.mechanism: Higher LAeq from unpleasant sources increases perceived discomfort.

findings.antecedent: A-weighted equivalent continuous sound level (LAeq) for pleasant children sounds (Experiment 1)
findings.mechanism: Higher LAeq from pleasant sources can slightly increase perceived comfort.
Higher LAeq generally leads to lower acoustic comfort.

findings.antecedent: Room acoustical parameters (C80, C50, EDT, STI, LF80, D50)
findings.mechanism: Models including individual room acoustical parameters were better than the basic model (sound source + random intercept), indicating their predictive power for acoustic comfort.
findings.quote: All models were better than the basic model with sound source and random intercept (without room acoustical parameters).

mechanisms: Sound is modified and articulated by the materiality and shape of surrounding surfaces, influencing acoustic comfort.
Absorptive materials reduce sound pressure levels and reflections, leading to increased acoustic comfort.
Balconies provide protection from noise sources, but reflective surfaces can weaken this effect.
Relatively pleasant sounds increase comfort, while unpleasant sounds decrease it.
Higher sound pressure levels (LAeq) are generally associated with lower acoustic comfort.
Stronger affective responses (very uncomfortable/comfortable) lead to faster, more automatic judgments.
Increased cumulative sound exposure over time (playback sequence) can lead to decreased comfort.
moderators: Sound source type (e.g., pleasant vs. unpleasant sounds)
Observer position (in yard vs. on balcony)
Balcony ceiling absorption (tendency observed when facade absorption is absent)
implementation_implications: Use materials with moderate absorption characteristics for facades or highly absorbing materials for selected facade portions to improve acoustic comfort.
Apply absorbing materials on balcony ceilings as a simple and cheap solution to improve acoustic comfort, especially when facade absorption is absent.

Design facilities that invite relatively pleasant sounds (e.g., playing children, water features, birds, vegetation) and avoid those encouraging unpleasant/noisy activities (e.g., basketball) to improve overall acoustic comfort in inner yards.

Architects, urban soundscape designers, and acousticians can use estimated room acoustical parameters (C50, C80, EDT, STI) to indicate subjective acoustic comfort and guide design changes for improved acoustic performance in housing complexes.

limitations: The room acoustical simulation method (ODEON) based on a geometrical approach has limitations (e.g., regarding diffraction).
The auralization was 2D (horizontal plane at ear level) instead of 3D.
The experiments did not include any visual stimuli, preventing investigation of aural-visual interactions.
There are general differences between laboratory experiments and on-site experience.
Most subjects worked for the authors' research institute, potentially introducing bias.
The study focused on short-term comfort, which differs from long-term comfort.
The study used single static sound sources, whereas reality typically involves a mixture of static and moving sounds.
The statistical models are not generalizable and require a larger amount of data and further validation for predictive purposes.
